notes: \cpara{Opens with hunter-gatherers, without a source, and with hedges (``usually,'' ``mostly,'' ``most''). The picture matches standard accounts. Wikipedia's article summarizes that hunter-gatherers ``tend to have an egalitarian social ethos,'' with settled groups such as those of the Northwest Coast of North America as exceptions. Richard Lee's ``Eating Christmas in the Kalahari'' (1969) describes the downplayed kill among the !Kung: the hunter says ``Ah, I'm no good for hunting. I saw nothing at all (pause) just a little tiny one.''}

\clogic{In Lee's account the reason is pride, and the others enforce the modesty. One of Lee's informants says: ``when a young man kills much meat he comes to think of himself as a chief or a big man \ldots\ So we always speak of his meat as worthless. This way we cool his heart and make him gentle.''}
\cpara{Argues that anyone who aims to do their best will sooner or later aim above the average.}

\cpara{The thesis: if you are ashamed of doing better than others, the median becomes ``your concrete wall.'' The opening example does not show this. Lee's hunter plays down his kill in public; his success is not in doubt, only the boast. Five paragraphs later the post itself calls public downplaying possibly ``the course of wisdom.'' No example or evidence is given of anyone who stopped improving at the median out of shame.}
\cpara{Allows that pride in doing better than others may be unhealthy, says it has been ``a useful motivator'' for the author, and defends such competition by comparison with Go.}

\clogic{The principles are probably those of ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' (2006), whose eighth virtue says ``spare no thought for whether others are doing worse'' and ``If you compare yourself to others you will not see the biases that all humans share.'' Two paragraphs later this post repeats that essay's ``life is not graded on a curve.''}
\cpara{Whatever the answer about pride, shame at doing better is not healthy.}

\cpara{A second reason, which sits uneasily with the first. Two paragraphs earlier, pride in doing better than others was a useful motivator. Here rank does not matter, and you should run ``without worrying that you might pull ahead of other runners.'' The post offers both, joined by ``And besides,'' and does not say how they fit together.}

\cpara{Predicts that progress will mean fixing flaws that most people have not fixed, and so having ``fewer sins to confess,'' an echo of the Yom Kippur confession in ``Tsuyoku Naritai!'', posted the day before.}
\cpara{Allows that it may be wise to downplay success in public (``People may forgive a touchdown, but not dancing in the end zone''), and mocks a show of modesty that everyone knows is untrue.}
\cpara{Says public modesty must not be the end: keep saying ``Tsuyoku'' to yourself, even in a whisper.}
\cpara{Reads the knowledge that you are still flawed as a reason to aim higher, ``without shame.''}
\cpara{Ends with a pledge to keep running as fast as possible, whether ahead or behind.}
